# Regional statistics institute

The statistics institute was opened in 1989 with charter authority to publish the
tabulations from censuses without clearing them first with any national agency. That
agency, the Statistics Council in Madrid, had refused to break out the figures below the
province level.

The institute has 42 people on staff. About half of them handle the decennial census,
and the rest tend to a historical archive that contains parish registers, which date
back to 1801 and municipal tax rolls since 1847.

## Funding

Regional government covers 71 percent of the institute's operating costs; the remainder
comes from contract work, mostly demographic projections for municipalities that need
them to plan construction projects such as new schools. The mix of funding has been
steady since 2011, though the portion from contracts swelled briefly to 40 percent when
the regional government slashed budgets in 2013 as austerity measures took effect.

## Access

The reading room where the public can access the institute's records is open Tuesday
through Friday. Researchers must have a letter of endorsement from their institution,
and you can order scans by post for 12 euros a page.

A 2024 audit by the regional comptroller found that 8 percent of the institute's
digitized records had errors in their metadata, mostly transposed dates in the returns
from 1901. The institute re-checked about a third of the affected records.

The institute's online catalog was last rebuilt in 2009 and cannot be searched by
parish. If researchers need help locating materials, institute staff do the lookup by
phone. But that process is likely to leave the archive effectively closed for someone
who does not understand Spanish or Catalan. The director, Marta Solé, wants to replace
the catalog before 2027, but there is currently no budget line for the work.

One concern is whether the metadata survives migration. She has noted that the institute
has batch-verified all of the records it has taken in one go, as the returns from 1901
all arrived in one donation. The scans were stored as TIFFs instead of JPEGs because the
conservators needed to retain a lossless master version.

Additional holdings included an atlas. Each ship comes with a separate sheet of paper
that has layered maps printed on it, including a regional inset for every one of the six
coastal parishes.

The handwritten notes on an ancillary system and its documentation mention only minimal
coverage in the regional press of an outage and refer to appendix B in the manual. The
post-1950 portion of the ledger uses the same numbering on the folios as the pre-1911
section. The green checkmark appears once when the job is finished and the release of the
final product has received legal approval.

A solid oak door, strong enough to lock with a stout ribbon, closes off the archive
below. The wax seal on the side of the cover of the 1911 folio is intact. The access
rules state that scans ship as TIFF, and that one divider separates the two eras in the
ledger below.
